entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen10294" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Evening Psalm in the Times of Absalom</title> <div sID="gen10295" type="x-p"/> The four Psalms, <reference osisRef="Ps.140.1-Ps.140.13">Psa 140:1-13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:1-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.7">Psa 142:1-7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.12">Psa 143:1-12</reference>, are interwoven with one another in many ways (<hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi>, pp. 67f.). The following passages are very similar, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.140.7">Psa 140:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1">Psa 141:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.2">Psa 142:2</reference>, and Psa 143:1. Just as the poet complains in <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference>, “when my spirit veils itself within me,” so too in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4">Psa 143:4</reference>; as he prays in Ps 142:8, “Oh bring my soul out of prison,” so in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.11">Psa 143:11</reference>, “bring my soul out of distress,” where צרה takes the place of the metaphorical מסגר. Besides these, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.140.5-Ps.140.6">Psa 140:5-6</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.141.9">Psa 141:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.7">Psa 142:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.143.9">Psa 143:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">Psa 140:3</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Psa 141:5</reference>, רעות; Ps 140:14 with Ps 142:8; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference> with Psa 143:8. <div eID="gen10295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10296" type="x-p"/> The right understanding of the Psalm depends upon the right understanding of the situation. Since it is inscribed לדוד, it is presumably a situation corresponding to the history of David, out of the midst of which the Psalm is composed, either by David himself or by some one else who desired to give expression in Davidic strains to David’s mood when in this situation. For the gleaning of Davidic Psalms which we find in the last two Books of the Psalter is for the most part derived from historical works in which these Psalms, in some instances only free reproductions of the feelings of David with respect to old Davidic models, adorned the historic narrative. The Psalm before us adorned the history of the time of the persecution by Absalom. At that time David was driven out of Jerusalem, and consequently cut off from the sacrificial worship of God upon Zion; and our Psalm is an evening hymn of one of those troublous days. The ancient church, even prior to the time of Gregory (<hi type="italic">Constitutiones Apostolicae</hi>, ii. 59), had chosen it for its evening hymn, just as it had chosen <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference> for its morning hymn. Just as <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference> was called ὁ ὀρθρινός (<hi type="italic">ibid</hi>. 8:37), so this Psalm, as being the Vesper Psalm, was called ὁ ἐπιλύχνιος (vid., 8:35).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.2">Psa 141:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10297" type="x-p"/> The very beginning of <reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:1-10</reference> is more after the manner of David than really Davidic; for instead of <hi type="italic">haste thee to me</hi>, David always says, <hi type="italic">haste thee for my help</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.20">Psa 22:20</reference>; 38:23; Psa 40:14. The לך that is added to בּקראי (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.4.2">Psa 4:2</reference>) is to be explained, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">Psa 57:3</reference> : when I call to Thee, i.e., when I call Thee, who art now far from me, to me. The general cry for help is followed in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference> by a petition for the answering of his prayer. Luther has given an excellent rendering: Let my prayer avail to Thee as an offering of incense; the lifting up of my hands, as an evening sacrifice (<hi type="italic">Mein Gebet müsse fur dir tügen wie ein Reuchopffer, Meine Hende auffheben, wie ein Abendopffer</hi>). תּכּון is the <hi type="italic">fut. Niph.</hi> of כּוּן, and signifies properly to be set up, and to be established, or reflexive: to place and arrange or prepare one’s self, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.12">Amo 4:12</reference>; then to continue, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.101.7">Psa 101:7</reference>; therefore, either let it place itself, let it appear, <hi type="italic">sistat se</hi>, or better: let it stand, continue, i.e., let my prayer find acceptance, recognition with Thee קטרת, and the lifting up of my hands מנחת־ערב. Expositors say that this in both instances is the <hi type="italic">comparatio decurtata</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Psa 11:1</reference> and elsewhere: as an incense-offering, as an evening <hi type="italic">mincha</hi>. But the poet purposely omits the כּ of the comparison. He wishes that God may be pleased to regard his prayer as sweet-smelling smoke or as incense, just as this was added to the <hi type="italic">azcara</hi> of the meal-offering, and gave it, in its ascending perfume, the direction upward to God,<note placement="foot">It is not the priestly קטרת תּמיד, i.e., the daily morning and evening incense-offering upon the golden altar of the holy place, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.8">Exo 30:8</reference>, that is meant (since it is a non-priest who is speaking, according to Hitzig, of course John Hyrcanus), but rather, as also in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa 1:13</reference>, the incense of the <hi type="italic">azcara</hi> of the meal-offering which the priest burnt (הקטיר) upon the altar; the incense (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.3">Isa 66:3</reference>) was entirely consumed, and not merely a handful taken from it.</note> and that He may be pleased to regard the lifting up of his hands (משׂאת, the construct with the reduplication given up, from משּׂאת, or even, after the form מתּנת, from משּׂאה, here not <hi type="italic">oblatio</hi>, but according to the phrase נשׂא כפּים ידים, <hi type="italic">elevatio</hi>, Jdg 20:38, Jdg 20:40, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>, and frequently) as an evening <hi type="italic">mincha</hi>, just as it was added to the evening <hi type="italic">tamı̂d</hi> according to <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38-Exod.29.42">Exo 29:38-42</reference>, and concluded the work of the service of the day.<note placement="foot">The reason of it is this, that the evening <hi type="italic">mincha</hi> is oftener mentioned than the morning <hi type="italic">mincha</hi> (see, however, 2Ki 3:20). The whole burnt-offering of the morning and the meat-offering of the evening (2Ki 16:15; 1Ki 18:29, 1Ki 18:36) are the beginning and close of the daily principal service; whence, according to the example of the <hi type="italic">usus</hi> <hi type="italic">loquendi</hi> in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan 9:21</reference>; Ezr 9:4., later on <hi type="italic">mincha</hi> directly signifies the afternoon or evening.</note>
entries.content_plain: Psa 141:1-2 The very beginning of Psa 141:1-10 is more after the manner of David than really Davidic; for instead of haste thee to me , David always says, haste thee for my help , Psa 22:20 ; 38:23; Psa 40:14. The לך that is added to בּקראי (as in Psa 4:2 ) is to be explained, as in Psa 57:3 : when I call to Thee, i.e., when I call Thee, who art now far from me, to me. The general cry for help is followed in Psa 141:2 by a petition for the answering of his prayer. Luther has given an excellent rendering: Let my prayer avail to Thee as an offering of incense; the lifting up of my hands, as an evening sacrifice ( Mein Gebet müsse fur dir tügen wie ein Reuchopffer, Meine Hende auffheben, wie ein Abendopffer ). תּכּון is the fut. Niph. of כּוּן, and signifies properly to be set up, and to be established, or reflexive: to place and arrange or prepare one’s self, Amo 4:12 ; then to continue, e.g., Psa 101:7 ; therefore, either let it place itself, let it appear, sistat se , or better: let it stand, continue, i.e., let my prayer find acceptance, recognition with Thee קטרת, and the lifting up of my hands מנחת־ערב. Expositors say that this in both instances is the comparatio decurtata , as in Psa 11:1 and elsewhere: as an incense-offering, as an evening mincha . But the poet purposely omits the כּ of the comparison. He wishes that God may be pleased to regard his prayer as sweet-smelling smoke or as incense, just as this was added to the azcara of the meal-offering, and gave it, in its ascending perfume, the direction upward to God, It is not the priestly קטרת תּמיד, i.e., the daily morning and evening incense-offering upon the golden altar of the holy place, Exo 30:8 , that is meant (since it is a non-priest who is speaking, according to Hitzig, of course John Hyrcanus), but rather, as also in Isa 1:13 , the incense of the azcara of the meal-offering which the priest burnt (הקטיר) upon the altar; the incense ( Isa 66:3 ) was entirely consumed, and not merely a handful taken from it. and that He may be pleased to regard the lifting up of his hands (משׂאת, the construct with the reduplication given up, from משּׂאת, or even, after the form מתּנת, from משּׂאה, here not oblatio , but according to the phrase נשׂא כפּים ידים, elevatio , Jdg 20:38, Jdg 20:40, cf. Psa 28:2 , and frequently) as an evening mincha , just as it was added to the evening tamı̂d according to Exo 29:38-42 , and concluded the work of the service of the day. The reason of it is this, that the evening mincha is oftener mentioned than the morning mincha (see, however, 2Ki 3:20). The whole burnt-offering of the morning and the meat-offering of the evening (2Ki 16:15; 1Ki 18:29, 1Ki 18:36) are the beginning and close of the daily principal service; whence, according to the example of the usus loquendi in Dan 9:21 ; Ezr 9:4., later on mincha directly signifies the afternoon or evening.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.141.3-Ps.141.4">Psa 141:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen10297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10298" type="x-p"/> The prayer now begins to be particularized, and that in the first instance as a petition fore the grace of silence, calling to mind old Davidic passages like <reference osisRef="Ps.39.2">Psa 39:2</reference>; Psa 34:14. The situation of David, the betrayed one, requires caution in speaking; and the consciousness of having sinned, not indeed against the rebels, but against God, who would not visit him thus without his deserving it, stood in the way of any outspoken self-vindication. In <hi type="italic">pone custodiam ori meo</hi> שׁמרה is ἅπ. λεγ., after the infinitive form דּבקה, עזבה, עצמה. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.141.3">Psa 141:3</reference></hi> דּל is ἅπ. λεγ. for דּלת; cf. “doors of the mouth” in Mic 7:5, and πύλαι στόματος in Euripides. נצּרה might be <hi type="italic">imper. Kal</hi>: keep I pray, with <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens</hi> as in Pro 4:13. But נצר על is not in use; and also as the parallel word to שׁמרה, which likewise has the appearance of being imperative, נצּרה is explicable as regards its pointing by a comparison of יקּהה in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, דּבּרה in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">Deu 33:3</reference>, and קרבה in Psa 73:28. The prayer for the grace of silence is followed in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.4">Psa 141:4</reference> by a prayer for the breaking off of all fellowship with the existing rulers. By a flight of irony they are called אישׁים, lords, in the sense of בּני אישׁ, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference> (cf. the Spanish <hi type="italic">hidalgos</hi> = <hi type="italic">hijos d'algo</hi>, sons of somebody). The evil thing (רע | דּבר, with <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> between the two ר, as in Num 7:13; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference> between the two מ, and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.3">1Ch 22:3</reference> between the two )ל, to which Jahve may be pleased never to incline his heart (תּט, <hi type="italic">fut. apoc.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.9">Psa 27:9</reference>), is forthwith more particularly designated: <hi type="italic">perpetrare facinora maligne cum dominis, etc.</hi> עללות of great achievements in the sense of infamous deeds, also occurs in <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>; Psa 99:8. Here, however, we have the <hi type="italic">Hithpo</hi>. התעלל, which, with the accusative of the object עללות, signifies: wilfully to make such actions the object of one’s acting (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">ta‛allala b - 'l - š'</hi>, to meddle with any matter, to amuse, entertain one’s self with a thing). The expression is made to express disgust as strongly as possible; this poet is fond of glaring colouring in his language. In the dependent passage <hi type="italic">neve eorum vescar cupediis, </hi>לחם is used poetically for אכל, and בּ is the partitive <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>, as in Job 21:25. מנעמּים is another hapaxlegomenon, but as being a designation of dainties (from נעם, to be mild, tender, pleasant), it may not have been an unusual word. It is a well-known thing that usurpers revel in the <hi type="italic">cuisine</hi> and cellars of those whom they have driven away.

In the dependent passage neve eorum vescar cupediis, לחם is used poetically for אכל, and בּ is the partitive Beth , as in Job 21:25. מנעמּים is another hapaxlegomenon, but as being a designation of dainties (from נעם, to be mild, tender, pleasant), it may not have been an unusual word. It is a well-known thing that usurpers revel in the cuisine and cellars of those whom they have driven away.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5-Ps.141.7">Psa 141:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen10298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10299" type="x-p"/> Thus far the Psalm is comparatively easy of exposition; but now it becomes difficult, yet not hopelessly so. David, thoroughly conscious of his sins against God and of his imperfection as a monarch, says, in opposition to the abuse which he is now suffering, that he would gladly accept any friendly reproof: “let a righteous man smite in kindness and reprove me - head-oil (i.e., oil upon the head, to which such reproof is likened) shall my head not refuse.” So we render it, following the accents, and not as Hupfeld, Kurtz, and Hitzig do: “if a righteous man smites me, it is love; if he reproves me, an anointing of the head is it unto me;” in connection with which the designation of the subject with היא would be twice wanting, which is more than is admissible. צדּיק stands here as an abstract substantive: the righteous man, whoever he may be, in antithesis, namely, to the rebels and to the people who have joined them. Amyraldus, Maurer, and Hengstenberg understand it of God; but it only occurs of God as an attribute, and never as a direct appellation. חסד, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jer 31:3</reference>, is equivalent to בּחסד, <hi type="italic">cum benignitate = benigne</hi>. What is meant is, as in <reference osisRef="Job.6.14">Job 6:14</reference>, what Paul (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.1">Gal 6:1</reference>) styles πνεῦμα πραΰ́τητος. and הלם, <hi type="italic">tundere</hi>, is used of the strokes of earnest but well-meant reproof, which is called “the blows of a friend” in Pro 27:6. Such reproof shall be to him as head-oil (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.133.2">Psa 133:2</reference>), which his head does not despise. יני, written defectively for יניא, like ישּׁי, in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference>, אבי, 1Ki 21:29 and frequently; הניא (root נא, Arab. <hi type="italic">n'</hi>, with the nasal <hi type="italic">n</hi>, which also expresses the negation in the Indo-Germanic languages) here signifies to deny, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.33.10">Psa 33:10</reference> to bring to nought, to destroy. On the other hand, the lxx renders μὴ λιπανάτω τὴν κεφαλήν μου, which is also followed by the Syriac and Jerome, perhaps after the Arabic <hi type="italic">nawiya</hi>, to become or to be fat, which is, however, altogether foreign to the Aramaic, and is, moreover, only used of fatness of the body, and in fact of camels. The meaning of the figure is this: well-meant reproof shall be acceptable and spiritually useful to him. The confirmation כּי־עוד וגו follows, which is enigmatical both in meaning and expression. This עוד is the cipher of a whole clause, and the following ו is related to this עוד as the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> that introduces the apodosis, not to כּי as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.20">2Ch 24:20</reference>, since no progression and connection is discernible if כי is taken as a subordinating <hi type="italic">quia</hi>. We interpret thus: <hi type="italic">for it is still so</hi> (the matter still stands thus), that my prayer is against their wickednesses; i.e., that I use no weapon but that of prayer against these, therefore let me always be in that spiritual state of mind which is alive to well-meant reproof. Mendelssohn’s rendering is similar: I still pray, whilst they practise infamy. On עוד ו cf. Zec 8:20 עוד אשׁר (vid., Köhler), and <reference osisRef="Prov.24.27">Pro 24:27</reference> אחר ו. He who has prayed God in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.3">Psa 141:3</reference> to set a watch upon his mouth is dumb in the presence of those who now have dominion, and seeks to keep himself clear of their sinful doings, whereas he willingly allows himself to be chastened by the righteous; and the more silent he is towards the world (see <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Amo 5:13</reference>), the more constant is he in his intercourse with God. But there will come a time when those who now behave as lords shall fall a prey to the revenge of the people who have been misled by them; and on the other hand, the confession of the salvation, and of the order of the salvation, of God, that has hitherto been put to silence, will again be able to make itself freely heard, and find a ready hearing. <div eID="gen10299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10300" type="x-p"/> As <reference osisRef="Ps.141.6">Psa 141:6</reference> says, the new rulers fall a prey to the indignation of the people and are thrown down the precipices, whilst the people, having again come to their right mind, obey the words of David and find them pleasant and beneficial (vid., <reference osisRef="Prov.15.26">Pro 15:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.24">Pro 16:24</reference>). נשׁמטוּ is to be explained according to 2Ki 9:33. The casting of persons down from the rock was not an unusual mode of execution (<reference osisRef="2Chr.25.12">2Ch 25:12</reference>). ידי־סלע are the sides (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.6">Psa 140:6</reference>; Jdg 11:26) of the rock, after which the expression ἐχόμενα πέτρας of the lxx, which has been misunderstood by Jerome, is intended to be understood;<note placement="foot">Beda Pieringer in his <hi type="italic">Psalterium Romana Lyra Radditum</hi> (Ratisbonae 1859) interprets κατεπόθησαν ἐχόμενα πέτρας οἱ κραταιοὶ τὐτῶν, <hi type="italic">absorpti</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">operti sunt loco ad petram pertinente signiferi turpis consilii eorum</hi>.</note> they are therefore the sides of the rock conceived of as it were as the hands of the body of rock, if we are not rather with Böttcher to compare the expressions בּידי and על־ידי construed with verbs of abandoning and casting down, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.14">Lam 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.11">Job 16:11</reference>, and frequently. In <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference> there follows a further statement of the issue on the side of David and his followers: <hi type="italic">instar findentis et secantis terram</hi> (בּקע with <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>, elsewhere in the hostile signification of <hi type="italic">irrumpere</hi>) <hi type="italic">dispersa sunt ossa nostra ad ostium</hi> (לפי as in <reference osisRef="Prov.8.3">Pro 8:3</reference>) <hi type="italic">orci</hi>; Symmachus: ὥσπερ γεωργὸς ὅταν ῥήσσῃ τὴν τὴν, οὕτως ἐσκορπίσθη τὰ ὀστᾶ ἡμῶν εἰς στόμα ᾅδου; Quinta: ὡς καλλιεργῶν καὶ σκάπτων ἐν τῇ γῇ κ. τ. λ. Assuming the very extreme, it is a look of hope into the future: should his bones and the bones of his followers be even scattered about the mouth of Sheôl (cf. the Syrian picture of Sheôl: “the dust upon its threshold <hi type="italic">‛al - escûfteh ,” Deutsche Morgenländ. Zeitschrift</hi>, xx. 513), their soul below, their bones above - it would nevertheless be only as when on in ploughing cleaves the earth; i.e., they do not lie there in order that they may continue lying, but that they may rise up anew, as the seed that is sown sprouts up out of the upturned earth. lxx <hi type="italic">Codd. Vat. et Sinait</hi>. τὰ ὀστᾶ ἡμῶν, beside which, however, is found the reading αὐτῶν (<hi type="italic">Cod. Alex.</hi> by a second hand, and the Syriac, Arabic, and Aethiopic versions), as Böttcher also, <hi type="italic">pro ineptissimo utcunque</hi>, thinks עצמינו must be read, understanding this, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.12">2Ch 25:12</reference> <hi type="italic">extrem</hi>., of the mangled bodies of those cast down from the rock. We here discern the hope of a resurrection, if not directly, at least (cf. Oehler in Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Real-Encyclopädie</hi>, concluding volume, S. 422) as am emblem of victory in spite of having succumbed. That which authorizes this interpretation lies in the figure of the husbandman, and in the conditional clause (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.8">Psa 141:8</reference>), which leads to the true point of the comparison; for as a complaint concerning a defeat that had been suffered: “so are our bones scattered for the mouth of the grave (in order to be swallowed up by it),” <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference>, would be alien and isolated with respect to what precedes and what follows.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.141.8-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen10300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10301" type="x-p"/> If <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Psa 141:7</reference> is not merely an expression of the complaint, but at the same time of hope, we now have no need to give the כּי the adversative sense of <hi type="italic">imo</hi>, but we may leave it its most natural confirmatory signification <hi type="italic">namque</hi>. From this point the Psalm gradually dies away in strains comparatively easy to be understood and in perfect keeping with the situation. In connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.141.8">Psa 141:8</reference> one is reminded of <reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">Psa 25:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">Psa 31:2</reference>; with Psa 141:9., of <reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.23">Psa 69:23</reference>, and other passages. In “pour not out (תּער with sharpened vowel instead of תּער, Ges. §75, rem. 8) my soul,” ערה, <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, is equivalent to the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הערה in Isa 53:12. ידי פח are as it were the hands of the seizing and capturing snare; and יקשׂוּ לּי is virtually a genitive: <hi type="italic">qui insidias tendunt mihi</hi>, since one cannot say יקשׁ פח, <hi type="italic">ponere laqueum</hi>. מכמרים, nets, in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.10">Psa 141:10</reference> is another hapaxlegomenon; the <hi type="italic">enallage numeri</hi> is as in <reference osisRef="Ps.62.5">Psa 62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.8">Isa 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">Isa 5:23</reference>, - the singular that slips in refers what is said of the many to each individual in particular. The plural מקשׁות for מקשׁים, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.6">Psa 18:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.6">Psa 64:6</reference>, also occurs only here. יחד is to be explained as in 4:9: it is intended to express the coincidence of the overthrow of the enemies and the going forth free of the persecuted one. With יחד אנכי the poet gives prominence to his simultaneous, distinct destiny: <hi type="italic">simul ego dum</hi> (עד as in <reference osisRef="Job.8.21">Job 8:21</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.1.18">Job 1:18</reference>) <hi type="italic">praetereo h.e. evado</hi>. The inverted position of the כּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10-Ps.18.12">Psa 18:10-12</reference> may be compared; with <reference osisRef="Ps.120.7">Psa 120:7</reference> and 2Ki 2:14, however (where instead of אף־הוּא it is with Thenius to be read אפוא), the case is different.  <chapter eID="Ps.141"/> <div eID="gen10301" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: Psa 141:8-10 If Psa 141:7 is not merely an expression of the complaint, but at the same time of hope, we now have no need to give the כּי the adversative sense of imo , but we may leave it its most natural confirmatory signification namque . From this point the Psalm gradually dies away in strains comparatively easy to be understood and in perfect keeping with the situation. In connection with Psa 141:8 one is reminded of Psa 25:15 ; Psa 31:2 ; with Psa 141:9., of Psa 7:16 ; Psa 69:23 , and other passages. In “pour not out (תּער with sharpened vowel instead of תּער, Ges. §75, rem. 8) my soul,” ערה, Piel , is equivalent to the Hiph . הערה in Isa 53:12. ידי פח are as it were the hands of the seizing and capturing snare; and יקשׂוּ לּי is virtually a genitive: qui insidias tendunt mihi , since one cannot say יקשׁ פח, ponere laqueum . מכמרים, nets, in Psa 141:10 is another hapaxlegomenon; the enallage numeri is as in Psa 62:5 ; Isa 2:8 ; Isa 5:23 , - the singular that slips in refers what is said of the many to each individual in particular. The plural מקשׁות for מקשׁים, Psa 18:6 ; Psa 64:6 , also occurs only here. יחד is to be explained as in 4:9: it is intended to express the coincidence of the overthrow of the enemies and the going forth free of the persecuted one. With יחד אנכי the poet gives prominence to his simultaneous, distinct destiny: simul ego dum (עד as in Job 8:21 , cf. Job 1:18 ) praetereo h.e. evado . The inverted position of the כּי in Psa 18:10-12 may be compared; with Psa 120:7 and 2Ki 2:14, however (where instead of אף־הוּא it is with Thenius to be read אפוא), the case is different.
entries.reader_content_plain: Psa 141:8-10 If Psa 141:7 is not merely an expression of the complaint, but at the same time of hope, we now have no need to give the כּי the adversative sense of imo , but we may leave it its most natural confirmatory signification namque . From this point the Psalm gradually dies away in strains comparatively easy to be understood and in perfect keeping with the situation. In connection with Psa 141:8 one is reminded of Psa 25:15 ; Psa 31:2 ; with Psa 141:9., of Psa 7:16 ; Psa 69:23 , and other passages.
